stem: An attacker has obtained username and password pairs from a breach of an unrelated service and is replaying them automatically against your firm's email provider. Which technique is this, and does multi-factor authentication defeat it?

choices.text: Phishing; MFA does not defeat it, because the one-time code is captured in the moment it is used.
Credential stuffing; MFA defeats it, because a correct password alone does not satisfy a second factor the attacker does not hold.
An infostealer; MFA does not defeat it, because the session cookie is taken after authentication has already happened.
Push bombing; MFA defeats it, because the subscriber can deny the prompt.

feedback: Credential stuffing replays pairs that were correct somewhere else, in the expectation that a share of people reused them. It is the one technique in this course that multi-factor authentication reliably defeats: the attacker holds only the password, and a second factor they cannot supply stops the login. If you chose one of the others, the gap is which attacks survive MFA — phishing, infostealers and attacks on the second factor all work against an account that has MFA switched on, which is what makes the rest of the course necessary. Re-read sections 03 and 05.

stem: You have followed a link to a page that appears to be your mail provider's sign-in screen. Which observation is actual evidence about who is on the other end of the connection?

choices.text: The page carries the provider's logo and its usual layout.
The browser shows a padlock or other connection-security indicator.
The address bar shows the provider's authenticated hostname, or a parent domain at least one level below the public suffix.
After signing in, the page forwards you to the genuine service.

feedback: The origin is the one thing on that list the authentication protocol itself binds to: for a DNS identifier, NIST identifies the verifier as its authenticated hostname or a parent domain at least one level below the public suffix (SP 800-63B-4, Sec. 3.2.5.2). A logo is a copied image and layout is copied markup, so (a) is evidence of nothing. A connection indicator tells you the connection is protected, not who terminates it — NIST prefers channel binding precisely because an impostor verifier may hold a certificate representing the real one (Sec. 3.2.5.1), which rules out (b). A well-built harvest page forwards the victim onward afterwards, so (d) is the attack working as designed rather than a reassurance. Re-read section 02, step two.

stem: An attacker has copied a valid session cookie out of a user's browser. When the attacker presents it, why does the service not ask for a second factor?

choices.text: Because the session cookie is itself an authenticator, and it satisfies the second factor on its own.
Because a second factor is only required the first time a given device signs in.
Because the cookie carries a session secret the service issued when authentication had already succeeded, so no authentication event is taking place.
Because multi-factor authentication is suspended for the duration of an established session.

feedback: The continuity of an authenticated session rests on possession of a session secret issued by the session host at the time of authentication (SP 800-63B-4, Sec. 5.1), and that secret is used as a bearer token. A service receiving a valid one sees an ordinary request on a running session, not an attempt to authenticate — and there is no authentication event for a second factor to attach to. Choice (a) inverts an explicit statement in Sec. 5.1.1: cookies are not authenticators, they are short-term secrets for the duration of a session. Choices (b) and (d) describe policies no source establishes. Re-read section 06.

stem: An attacker's site relays an entire sign-in to the genuine service as it happens, passing each prompt and answer through in real time. Which property of an authentication method defeats that attack?

choices.text: The authenticator output changes on every use, so a captured value cannot be replayed later.
The subscriber must type a number shown by the identity platform into the authenticator application.
The authenticator output is cryptographically bound to the channel, or to the verifier's authenticated name, so an output produced at the attacker's site is not valid at the real one.
The subscriber is trained to inspect the address bar before entering any code.

feedback: Phishing resistance requires cryptographic authentication and is achieved either by channel binding or by verifier name binding (SP 800-63B-4, Sec. 3.2.5). Choice (a) describes replay resistance, which one-time-password authenticators genuinely have (Sec. 3.2.7) — it is simply beside the point, because the proxy uses the code now, inside its validity window, not tomorrow. Choice (b) is number matching, which CISA rates resistant to push bombing but still vulnerable to phishing; the proxy can read the number off the real service and show it to the victim. Choice (d) fails NIST's own test, which requires resistance without relying on the vigilance of the claimant. Re-read sections 07 and 09.

stem: Which signal does SP 800-63B-4 require a provider to send to a subscriber for the express purpose of letting that subscriber detect fraud on their own account?

choices.text: An independent notification that an authenticator was bound to the account, or that account recovery was started.
A monthly summary of the account's storage and activity totals.
A prompt to choose a new password because ninety days have passed since the last change.
A warning that the browser or operating system is out of date.

feedback: Section 4.6 requires that certain subscriber account events — NIST's own examples are the binding of an authenticator and account recovery — cause the subscriber, or someone they designate, to be independently notified, and it states the purpose outright: these notifications help the subscriber detect possible fraud. That is what makes an unexpected “a new sign-in method was added” message the strongest indicator available to an individual, rather than routine noise. Choice (c) describes scheduled password expiry, which Sec. 3.1.1.2 now prohibits — a change must be forced on evidence of compromise, not on the calendar. Re-read section 10.

stem: You suspect an account has been taken over and that the attacker may be holding a stolen session. Of the actions below, which should come first, and for what reason?

choices.text: Change the password, because a new password ends the attacker's access to the account.
Terminate the sessions, because a password change does not by itself end a session that is already running.
Re-enrol the authenticators, because the attacker may have bound one you did not add.
Report the incident, because reporting has to precede any remediation.

feedback: A session's continuity rests on a secret issued when authentication succeeded, not on the password (SP 800-63B-4, Sec. 5.1), and a new password governs only the next authentication event — so changing it first can leave the stolen session running untouched. CISA, NSA, the FBI and MS-ISAC likewise put re-provisioning a compromised account first among their incident response steps, in order to prevent malicious actors from maintaining continued access. Choices (a) and (c) are both real steps and both belong in the response; they follow rather than lead. Remember too that sessions at an identity provider and at a relying party terminate independently (Sec. 5.2), so one sign-out is not a global act. Re-read sections 06 and 11.

stem: A staff member signs in to a cloud document store through the firm's single sign-on service. The single sign-on service is the system that checks the password and the security key; the document store then opens the client workpapers. In the vocabulary SP 800-63B-4 uses, what is each of those two systems?

choices.text: The document store is the verifier and the single sign-on service is the relying party.
The single sign-on service is the verifier and the document store is the relying party.
Both are verifiers, because each of them requires the staff member to be signed in.
Both are relying parties, because neither of them holds the staff member's authenticators.

feedback: A verifier is the entity that confirms the claimant's identity by verifying their possession and control of one or more authenticators — that is the single sign-on service, because it is the system the password and the security key are presented to. A relying party is the entity that relies on a verifier's assertion of identity, typically to grant access to information or a system — that is the document store, which never sees the authenticators and acts on the assertion instead. Choice (a) reverses the two. Choice (c) confuses being signed in with checking the authenticators; only one system does the checking. Choice (d) is the same error in the other direction — the fact that a system does not hold your authenticators is exactly what makes it a relying party rather than a verifier, so it cannot make both of them one. The distinction is worth holding on to: it is why signing out of one service does not sign you out of the other, which section 11 depends on. Re-read section 01, “The words this course uses.”
_source: sources/sec/NIST-SP-800-63B-4.txt App. D (the glossary entries for verifier and relying party, quoted in the section); §5.2 (an IdP and an RP manage sessions separately). No flag inherited — drafts/SEC-01-review.md records no UNSOURCED flag on sec-01's definitions.

stem: NIST's definition of multi-factor authentication requires more than one distinct type of authentication factor, and it names three types: something you know, something you have, and something you are. Which of these arrangements satisfies that definition?

choices.text: A password, plus a numeric PIN the subscriber chose for the same account.
A password, plus a one-time code delivered to an authenticator app on the subscriber's phone.
A password, plus the answer to a security question about a first pet or a first school.
A password, re-entered on a second device in order to confirm it.

feedback: The word doing the work in the definition is *type*. Two of something you know is not multi-factor, however many secrets are involved. A password is something you know, and SP 800-63B-4 treats a numeric password as a PIN, so (a) is one type twice. The answer to a security question is another remembered secret, so (c) is too — and NIST separately forbids verifiers from prompting subscribers to use knowledge-based authentication or security questions when choosing passwords (Sec. 3.1.1.2). Choice (d) changes the device, not the factor; the same secret is still the only thing being proved. In (b) the code arrives on a device the subscriber possesses and controls, which is something you have, so two distinct types are in play. Note what this question does not say: satisfying the definition is not the same as being safe against the attacks in sections 06 through 08. Re-read section 05.
_source: sources/sec/NIST-SP-800-63B-4.txt App. D (“multi-factor authentication” and “authentication factor” — the three types); §3.1.1 (“A password (sometimes referred to as a passphrase or, if numeric, a personal identification number [PIN])… A password is ‘something you know.’”); §3.1.3 (“An out-of-band authenticator is ‘something you have.’”); §3.1.1.2 item 8 (no KBA or security questions). No flag inherited — sec-05's two flags are on the “test applied at one moment” framing and the six-digit-code paraphrase, neither of which this question rests on.

stem: An attacker holds a stolen session cookie and is actively working inside the account. Under the session management requirements of SP 800-63B-4, what actually limits how long that stolen session remains usable?

choices.text: The overall timeout, since the attacker's own activity keeps resetting the inactivity timeout.
The inactivity timeout, since a session in continuous use is not subject to any overall limit.
Nothing in the protocol; a session secret stays valid until the subscriber signs out.
Nothing in the protocol; presenting the cookie is a fresh authentication event and restarts both clocks.

feedback: Two timeouts run on a session. An overall timeout limits its duration since authentication or since the last reauthentication, and an inactivity timeout ends a session that goes quiet. When either expires the session must be terminated — but session activity resets the inactivity timeout, and the attacker is generating activity, so the inactivity clock never runs down while they are working. That leaves the overall timeout as the one that actually bites, which is why (b) is the wrong half of the pair. Choice (c) understates the protocol: logout does invalidate the secret, but it is not the only thing that ends a session. Choice (d) is the misunderstanding this whole section exists to remove — presenting a session secret is not authenticating, which is precisely why no second factor is asked for and why nothing about it restarts the overall clock. Re-read section 06, “What limits the damage.”
_source: sources/sec/NIST-SP-800-63B-4.txt §5.2 (the two timeouts; “When either timeout expires, the session SHALL be terminated. Session activity SHALL reset the inactivity timeout…”); §5.1 (session secrets erased or invalidated at logout). No flag inherited — sec-06's two flags are on the bearer-token gloss and the “no point in the flow” sentence, and this question rests on neither.

stem: Section 3.1.3 of SP 800-63B-4 rules out one form of out-of-band authentication that used to be ordinary, and it does so because of authentication fatigue. What is the test that separates the arrangements NIST still permits from the one it no longer accepts?

choices.text: Which way the secret travels: NIST now permits only a secret sent to the phone, never one read off it.
Whether the subscriber transfers the secret between the two channels, or merely compares two values and approves.
How long the secret is: six digits is no longer sufficient for an out-of-band authenticator.
Which carrier the second channel uses: a push notification is permitted where a text message is not.

feedback: NIST permits two arrangements, and both of them are transfers: the subscriber moves a secret received on the out-of-band device into the primary channel, or moves a secret shown in the primary channel onto the out-of-band device. What it rules out is the third arrangement, in which the two channels each display a value and the subscriber taps approve — no longer acceptable, because it makes it likelier that the subscriber approves without actually comparing, as has been seen in authentication fatigue attacks. So the test is transfer versus compare-and-approve. Choice (a) is the most tempting error, because transfer in either direction is permitted; the direction is not the point. Choices (c) and (d) name properties NIST does not use to draw this line. One extra line is worth knowing when you look at a real product: being shown a short list of values to pick from is not sufficient either, because the list is small enough to guess. Re-read section 08, “Where NIST now goes further.”
_source: sources/sec/NIST-SP-800-63B-4.txt §3.1.3 (the two permitted transfer arrangements; the note that the third method — comparing the secrets and requesting approval — “is no longer considered acceptable”, its authentication-fatigue rationale, and the limited-size-of-the-list sentence); App. E change log. No flag inherited — sec-08's four flags are the two composed scenarios, the nagging-mechanism inference and the closing aphorism; this question rests on the NIST text directly.

stem: A four-partner practice has decided to move to phishing-resistant multi-factor authentication. CISA's fact sheet names two implementations of it. Which one does CISA identify as the realistic choice for an organisation of that size?

choices.text: PKI-based MFA, because CISA treats smart cards as the stronger of the two and recommends them first.
FIDO/WebAuthn, because CISA calls it the only widely available phishing-resistant authentication.
Either one — CISA rates the two as equally deployable and leaves the choice to the organisation.
Neither — CISA advises a practice this small to stay on app-based one-time passwords for now.

feedback: CISA names FIDO/WebAuthn as the only widely available phishing-resistant authentication, and support for it is built into the major browsers, operating systems and phones. It describes PKI-based MFA as providing strong security and being sensible for large and complex organisations, but adds that deploying it successfully requires highly mature identity management practices and that it is not as widely supported by commonly used services — which is what makes (a) and (c) wrong, and which is a statement about deployability rather than about strength. Choice (d) inverts CISA's advice: it urges organisations to prioritise phishing-resistant MFA for administrator and privileged accounts and to begin with the services that already support it, noting that most hosted mail and single sign-on systems support FIDO. Re-read section 09, “What is actually deployable.”
_source: sources/sec/CISA-Implementing-Phishing-Resistant-MFA.pdf, “Phishing-Resistant MFA Implementations” (“The only widely available phishing-resistant authentication is FIDO/WebAuthn authentication”; PKI-based MFA “requires highly mature identity management practices” and “is also not as widely supported by commonly used services”) and “Areas of Focus” (prioritise administrator and privileged accounts; most hosted mail and SSO systems support FIDO). No flag inherited — sec-09's two flags are the lo-4 payoff sentence and the closing aphorism, and this question rests on neither.

stem: A practice's IT checklist requires every password to contain an uppercase letter, a digit and a symbol. Under SP 800-63B-4, what is the standing of that requirement?

choices.text: Required — mixing character types is how a password meets NIST's strength expectations.
Permitted but discouraged; NIST leaves password composition to each organisation's own policy.
Prohibited — verifiers shall not impose composition rules, because users answer them predictably.
Prohibited for a password used as a single factor, but still required inside a multi-factor process.

feedback: SP 800-63B-4 states it twice: other composition requirements for passwords shall not be imposed (Sec. 3.1.1.1), and verifiers and CSPs shall not impose composition rules such as requiring mixtures of different character types (Sec. 3.1.1.2). Appendix A gives the reason, and it is the reason that matters in practice: users respond to composition rules in very predictable ways, so someone who would have chosen “password” chooses “Password1” when an uppercase letter and a digit are demanded, and “Password1!” when a symbol is added — which moves the password to exactly the place an attacker already looks. Choice (a) is the belief the rule was written to displace; length and blocklist screening carry the strength, not character classes. Choice (b) understates a SHALL NOT. Choice (d) invents a split the standard does not make — the length minimum differs between single-factor and multi-factor use, but the prohibition on composition rules does not. This is the part of the guidance most likely to be out of date in a checklist or a vendor default, so check it against Sec. 3.1.1.2 before adopting it. Re-read section 03, “What the current requirement actually says.”
_source: sources/sec/NIST-SP-800-63B-4.txt §3.1.1.1 (“Other composition requirements for passwords SHALL NOT be imposed.”); §3.1.1.2 item 5 (verifiers and CSPs shall not impose composition rules) and item 1 (the 15/8-character split, for choice (d)); App. A.3 (the “password” → “Password1” → “Password1!” reasoning, quoted closely). No flag inherited — sec-03's three flags are all interpretive and sit on the stuffing/blocklist connection, the untouched-practice claim and the word “unique”; none of them is this question's ground.
